long_biography.plain_text:
Born in Cincinnati into the family that built Fleischmann's Yeast, Max Charles Fleischmann joined the company at eighteen and advanced through manufacturing and executive posts. Army service left him widely known as Major. After his brother's death, he ran the yeast and distilling business and became its chairman, while also handling family real-estate and investment interests.

Fleischmann helped steer the company into the merger that created Standard Brands, where he remained chairman for several years. At his death, his wealth was still rooted in inherited food-business ownership that he had expanded through management and investment. He had created a charitable foundation, and most of his estate later passed into it under trust terms. The foundation's principal, subsequent investment growth and grants belonged to the institution rather than to Fleischmann personally.

uncertainties.detail: Major is a military title rather than a given name. The source display name remains accurate, while the proposed structured fields restore Max as first name and Charles as middle name. The optional blank title field is not proposed because the inventory does not classify it as researchable.

University of Nevada authority uses Max Charles, while some secondary records expand Max as Maximilian or Maximillian. The proposed structured name uses Max Charles, the form supported by the strongest archival authority, and retains the established display form Max C.

Archival and government sources securely establish 1877-1951, Ohio birth and age 74. The exact 26 February and 16 October dates rely on matching historical biographical records, so those component proposals carry high rather than very-high confidence.

Fleischmann had left the Standard Brands chairmanship well before death and held investments and property. Food and Beverage remains the best primary-industry classification because the inherited and expanded food company generated the fortune and no later sector is shown to have displaced it.

Historical estate estimates are omitted. Property held by his executors was estate property after death, while foundation principal, later investment appreciation and grants belonged to the charitable institution rather than to Fleischmann personally.
